title: Cancellation and timeouts
sub: CancellationToken: a polite request to stop
cards/0/body:
Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: a CancellationTokenSource hands out a token (CancellationToken), you pass it to methods, and they check it themselves and stop working. You can't forcibly "kill" a task.

A source can be created with a timeout: new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)) cancels its token by itself after 5 seconds. To cancel manually, call cts.Cancel().

A method that notices cancellation throws OperationCanceledException. The async method's task then goes into the Canceled state (not Faulted), and awaiting that task throws OperationCanceledException again. HttpClient throws its subclass, TaskCanceledException, so catch (OperationCanceledException) catches it too.
cards/1/q: The server didn't reply within 5 seconds. What happens?
cards/1/options/0: The token is canceled, and await throws OperationCanceledException (more precisely, its subclass TaskCanceledException)
cards/1/explain: After 5 seconds the source cancels the token by itself. HttpClient, which received the token, aborts the request, its task becomes Canceled, and await throws TaskCanceledException, a subclass of OperationCanceledException.
cards/2/title: Your own code must listen to the token too
cards/2/body:
cts.Cancel() only sets a flag in the token and calls its subscribers. Code finds out about cancellation at the next check: ThrowIfCancellationRequested() throws OperationCanceledException, and HttpClient, the file API or a database driver that received the token abort the operation themselves.

So in a long loop, check the token between steps and pass it on to every async method. Otherwise cancellation gets stuck at your method.

Methods receive the token, not the source: the receiver can only listen, and only the owner of the CancellationTokenSource can cancel.
cards/3/q: An import loop: cts.Cancel() is called while the synchronous Parse(text) is running. When does the method stop?
cards/3/options/0: When Parse finishes: at the next ThrowIfCancellationRequested check
cards/3/options/2: Never: cancellation is noticed only at the start of a method
cards/3/explain: Cancel only sets a flag. Parse doesn't check the token, so it runs to the end, and on the next iteration ThrowIfCancellationRequested throws OperationCanceledException.
cards/4/explain: SaveAsync didn't get the token: a save in progress won't be interrupted.
cards/5/title: When a method doesn't take a token
cards/5/body:
You can't stop someone else's operation without a token; you can only stop waiting for it.

task.WaitAsync(ct) and task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan) (.NET 6+) return a task that completes together with the original one, or earlier: with OperationCanceledException on the token, or with TimeoutException on the timeout.

The operation itself keeps running in the background, and nobody will see its result or its error.
cards/5/code:
var t = legacy.DownloadAsync(url);                       // takes no token
var data = await t.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));   // TimeoutException after 5 s
cards/6/q: How do you cancel a task that doesn't accept a token?
cards/6/options/0: Not directly: you can only stop waiting for it, e.g. with WaitAsync(token)
cards/6/explain: WaitAsync stops the waiting, but the operation itself keeps running in the background. A Task has no way to stop someone else's code from the outside.
cards/7/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/2: A CancellationTokenSource can be created with a timeout
cards/7/options/4: Checking the token at the end of the method is enough
cards/7/explain: Code stops only where it checks the token. A check at the end of the method is useless: the work is already done by then.
cards/8/explain: Methods receive the token itself, not the source: only its owner should cancel.
